title: Definition Unit Tests Improve LLM Convention Adherence

contributions.purpose: Improve LLM adherence to a specified convention when multiple valid conventions exist.
contributions.mechanism: Definition Unit Tests (DUT): a training-free prompt wrapper prepending k=3 discriminative verified fact checks (question-answer pairs whose answers differ across conventions) derived from the same glossary, binding the model to the glossary semantics before the main problem.
contributions.evaluation: On ErdosConventionsBench (300 items, greedy decoding), DUT improves accuracy +5.0pp on Qwen2.5-Math-7B (95.0% vs 90.0%) and +22.7pp on Llama-3.1-8B (81.3% vs 58.7%) over engagement-matched baselines.
contributions.domain: Prompt engineering for convention/definition adherence in mathematical reasoning
contributions.source_quote: We propose Definition Unit Tests, a training-free method that uses discriminative definition checks to improve LLM convention adherence.

contributions.purpose: Isolate the effect of discriminative content from generic added computation.
contributions.mechanism: Engagement-matched experimental framework with a neutral-checks baseline (Condition B) adding k facts whose answers do not distinguish conventions, plus majority-vote (A@5, B@5) comparisons.
contributions.evaluation: Neutral checks stay within 2pp of glossary-only; DUT beats majority vote using a single generation (+53.7pp over A@5, +44.3pp over B@5 on Qwen), confirming discriminative content, not compute, drives gains.
contributions.domain: Experimental design / confound control for prompting studies
contributions.source_quote: We design an engagement-matched experimental framework with neutral-checks baselines that rules out computation as a confound, isolating the effect of discriminative content.

contributions.purpose: Characterize the mechanism and when DUT helps most versus when errors are non-convention.
contributions.mechanism: Measure alternate-convention match rate, per-family accuracy, effect of number of checks k, and error analysis distinguishing convention vs computational errors.
contributions.evaluation: DUT cuts alternate-convention match rate ~80% (7.0%->1.3% Qwen, 9.3%->2.0% Llama); largest gains on completeness family (+61pp Llama); convolution barely improves on Llama since 29% of errors are arithmetic, not convention.
contributions.source_quote: The alternate-convention match rate confirms the mechanism: DUT reduces the fraction of answers matching the wrong convention from 7.0% to 1.3% on Qwen (81% relative reduction) and from 9.3% to 2.0% on Llama (78% relative reduction).

self_declared_provenance.quote: DUT extends this line of work by using discriminative checks to actively verify that models have correctly bound to the provided convention definition before solving the main problem.
DUT shares the philosophy of using tests to verify behavior, but applies this principle to convention adherence in mathematical reasoning rather than code generation.

The key insight is that definitions can be treated as semantic contracts: just as software contracts are enforced through test cases designed to fail under common misinterpretations, glossary definitions can be tested using questions whose answers differ under alternate conventions.
We evaluate DUT on ErdosConventionsBench, a synthetic benchmark derived from mathematical conventions on ErdosProblems.com (Feng et al., 2026).
